info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,

info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.

The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: A flat, polished section of as-built laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg was imaged in a Thermo Fisher Apreo SEM at 5.00 kV, 0.10 nA, 9.75 mm working distance with the chamber Everhart-Thornley detector (ETD; the data bar does not say whether it was in SE mode with a positively biased collector grid or in BSE mode). A dedicated BSE detector showed the same bright and dark features with the same grayscale ordering.
Questions:
(1) What fraction of an ETD image in SE mode is derived from backscattered electrons: direct BSE reaching the scintillator, SE2 generated by BSE leaving the specimen surface, and SE3 generated by BSE striking the pole piece and chamber walls? Give literature measurements (e.g. Peters; Reimer; Goldstein et al.; Seiler; Joy) and how this split changes for a light matrix such as Al (Z=13) and at low beam energy (about 5 kV). Is the total SE yield itself Z-dependent through the SE2 term (delta_total = delta_SE1 (1 + beta*eta))?
(2) Does an ETD SE-mode image therefore show atomic-number (BSE-like) contrast on a flat polished multiphase specimen, and how large is it compared with a dedicated BSE detector? Is it correct to say that ETD SE images 'cannot tell whether a feature is heavier than the matrix'?
(3) Besides higher mean atomic number, what makes a sub-micron feature brighter than the Al matrix in ETD images (edge and topographic effects, negative charging of insulating particles such as alumina, silica, SiC or diamond, contamination)? If a dedicated BSE detector (Apreo in-lens T1 or a retractable annular/CBS detector) shows the same bright features, how strongly does that establish a higher mean Z rather than topography or charging?
(4) At 5 kV, what are the backscatter coefficients (or the ordering) of Al, Si, Al2O3, SiO2, SiC, C (diamond), Mg2Si, Fe-rich Al-Fe-Si intermetallics (beta-Al5FeSi, alpha-Al15(Fe,Mn)3Si2) and Fe? Are the orderings known from 20-30 kV preserved at 5 kV, or are there contrast compressions or reversals at low kV?
Cite primary literature and textbooks, and say clearly where evidence is missing.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-part question about SEM imaging of AlSi10Mg, ETD detector physics, and backscatter coefficients.

Abstract:
Information in SEM images about specimen properties is conveyed when contrast in the backscattered and/or secondary electron signals is created by differences in the interaction of the beam electrons between a specimen feature and its surroundings. Abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The long‐standing view in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) holds that SE1 electrons determine image resolution, whereas SE2 electrons contribute mainly to the background. However, the quantitative relationship between SE1/SE2 emission and spatial resolution has never been rigorously established due to the lack of explicit definitions for SE1 and SE2 for a Monte Carlo simulation. In this study, we develop a comprehensive simulation framework with unambiguous SE1/SE2 definitions to investigate secondary electron emission from typical solid materials by a 0.1–30 keV primary beam. The results reveal that SE1 and SE2 exhibit no intrinsic difference in emission characteristics except for the spatial spreading, and the local 3D morphology of the surface shall modulate SE2 spatial emission. Simulations for Au nanoparticles on a carbon substrate illustrate that the morphology‐modulated SE2 electrons near particle edges contribute significantly to sub‐nanometer resolution (∼0.8 nm); the exclusion of SE3 by the in‐lens detector also plays a role in resolution enhancement. This work overturns the conventional consideration that SE2 degrades resolution, and provides a unified physical explanation for the mechanism of ultrahigh‐resolution SEM imaging.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Scanning electron microscopy is widespread in field of material science and research, especially because of its high surface sensitivity due to the increased interactions of electrons with the target material’s atoms compared to X-ray-oriented methods. Among the available techniques in scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) is used to gather information regarding the crystallinity and the chemistry of crystalline and amorphous regions of a specimen. When post-processing the diffraction patterns or the image captured by the EBSD detector screen which was obtained in this manner, specific imaging contrasts are generated and can be used to understand some of the mechanisms involved in several imaging modes. In this manuscript, we reviewed the benefits of this procedure regarding topographic, compositional, diffraction, and magnetic domain contrasts. This work shows preliminary and encouraging results regarding the non-conventional use of the EBSD detector. The method is becoming viable with the advent of new EBSD camera technologies, allowing acquisition speed close to imaging rates. This method, named dark-field electron backscatter diffraction imaging, is described in detail, and several application examples are given in reflection as well as in transmission modes.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This chapter provides guidance on designing laboratory practices for material characterization using electron microscopy, with a focus on the advantages of using backscattered electrons (BSE), secondary electrons (SE), and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The approach includes insights into using other microscopy techniques such as atomic force microscopy (AFM), ellipsometry, and optical profilometry as complementary methods to validate results from electron microscopy. Examples of applications include eutectic alloys, thermal oxides, and nanoparticles in various industries. Successful syllabuses for undergraduate and graduate courses are illustrated, and the laboratory teachings’ results were presented at a conference and published in peer-reviewed journals.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract 2018 marked the 50th anniversary of the introduction of energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS) with semiconductor detectors to electron-excited X-ray microanalysis. Initially useful for qualitative analysis, EDS has developed into a fully quantitative analytical tool that can match wavelength dispersive spectrometry for accuracy in the determination of major (mass concentration C > 0.1) and minor (0.01 ≤ C ≤ 0.1) constituents, and useful accuracy can extend well into the trace (0.001 < C < 0.01) constituent range even when severe peak interference occurs. Accurate analysis is possible for low atomic number elements (B, C, N, O, and F), and at low beam energy, which can optimize lateral and depth spatial resolution. By recording a full EDS spectrum at each picture element of a scan, comprehensive quantitative compositional mapping can also be performed.

Abstract:
Abstract. Background: Charging of insulators is a complex phenomenon to simulate since the accuracy of the simulations is very sensitive to the interaction of electrons with matter and electric fields. Aim: In this study, we report model improvements for a previously developed Monte-Carlo simulator to more accurately simulate samples that charge. Approach: The improvements include both modeling of low energy electron scattering by first-principle approaches and charging of insulators by the redistribution of the charge carriers in the material with an electron beam-induced conductivity and a dielectric breakdown model. Results: The first-principle scattering models provide a more realistic charge distribution cloud in the material and a better match between noncharging simulations and experimental results. The improvements on the charging models, which mainly focus on the redistribution of the charge carriers, lead to a smoother distribution of the charges and better experimental agreement of charging simulations. Conclusions: Combined with a more accurate tracing of low energy electrons in the electric field, we managed to reproduce the dynamically changing charging contrast due to an induced positive surface potential.

Abstract:
The imaging of non-conducting materials by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is most often performed after depositing few nanometers thick conductive layers on the samples. It is shown in this work, that even a 5 nm thick sputtered gold layer can dramatically alter the morphology and the surface structure of many different types of aerogels. Silica, polyimide, polyamide, calcium-alginate and cellulose aerogels were imaged in their pristine forms and after gold sputtering utilizing low voltage scanning electron microscopy (LVSEM) in order to reduce charging effects. The morphological features seen in the SEM images of the pristine samples are in excellent agreement with the structural parameters of the aerogels measured by nitrogen adsorption-desorption porosimetry. In contrast, the morphologies of the sputter coated samples are significantly distorted and feature nanostructured gold. These findings point out that extra care should be taken in order to ensure that gold sputtering does not cause morphological artifacts. Otherwise, the application of low voltage scanning electron microscopy even yields high resolution images of pristine non-conducting aerogels.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Partially wetting water droplets with sizes smaller than the capillary length acquire a distinct spherical cap shape controlled by the equilibrium contact angle, which is specific for different substrates and conditions. Images of such droplets in an environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) show strong topographic contrast. This contrast across the droplets can be analysed within a simple theoretical model, as the droplet sides are inclined smooth surfaces. Very small droplets have ESEM intensity profiles which deviate from this topographic model. Such deviations indicate that other sources of electron signal may be important for such droplets, and also demonstrate the limits of the analytical model. For droplets sufficiently large that they lie within the range of the topographic contrast model, values of contact angles on different substrates can be deduced. These are found to agree with independent direct measurements, as well as the results given in the literature. The possibilities of using this technique to analyse physical properties of different substrates are discussed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this work, plasma electrolytic oxidation (PEO) process was applied on AlSi10Mg samples, produced with laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF), in the as printed condition and after different heat treatments, and, for comparison, on as-cast samples of AlSi10Mg. PEO process was performed in direct-current mode using high current densities and short time in a basic silicate electrolyte. For the first time, the effects of silicon morphology in L-PBF AlSi10Mg samples, in as printed condition and after different heat treatments, on the obtained PEO coating were investigated in terms of microstructure and corrosion properties. The microstructure of the substrate was characterized with optical and electron microscopy observations (optical microscopy OM, scanning electron microscopy SEM, and transmission electron microscopy TEM) and with X-ray diffraction (XRD). The analysis showed that heat treatments of annealing and solution treating modified the morphology and distribution of silicon in the samples obtained through L-PBF. The PEO coated samples were characterized with SEM, both on the surface and in the cross-section, and compositional analysis were performed with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) analysis and elemental mapping. The coatings were also analyzed with XRD and the corrosion properties evaluated through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. Also microhardness tests were performed on the substrates and on the coatings. The microstructure of the coatings was strongly influenced by the silicon distribution. In particular, a non-uniform distribution of silicon and the presence of iron-rich intermetallic (obtained in the as-cast and solution treated samples) induced the formation of more porous and thinner coatings in comparison with the ones obtained in the as printed and annealed samples. The not-uniform silicon distribution produced a not-homogenous distribution of silicon into the coatings. The particular cellular structure of the as printed sample induced the formation of a coating with a higher amorphous fraction, in comparison with the ones produced on the other samples. The higher thickness and lower porosity of the coatings obtained on the annealed and as printed samples resulted in an increase of the corrosion resistance.

Abstract:
The present study aims to investigate the microstructural evolution and local mechanical properties of an AlFe18Si8Cr5Ni2 alloy processed via Powder Bed Fusion–Laser-Based Manufacturing (PBF-LB/M). Designed with a focus on sustainability, this alloy was produced by deriving the necessary elements from AlSi10Mg and 304L steel, two of the most widely used alloys and, consequently, among the easiest materials to source from machining scrap. By leveraging iron, chromium, and nickel from these widespread standard compositions, the alloy mitigates the detrimental effects of Fe contamination in Al-based alloys while simultaneously enhancing mechanical performance. A comprehensive investigation of the impact of rapid solidification and thermal cycling offered novel insights into phase stability, elemental distribution, and local mechanical behavior. In particular, microstructural analyses using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), field emission SEM, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and differential scanning calorimetry revealed significant phase modifications post PBF-LB/M processing, including Fe-rich acicular phase segregation at melt pool boundaries and enhanced strengthening phase formation. In addition, nanoindentation mapping was used to demonstrate the correlation between microstructural heterogeneity and local mechanical properties. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of Al-Fe-Si-Cr-Ni alloy changes after the interaction with the laser, supporting the development of high-performance, sustainable Al-based materials for PBF-LB/M applications.

Abstract:
Cooling Rate (CR) definitively influences the microstructure of metallic parts manufactured through various processes. Factors including cooling medium, surface area, thermal conductivity, and temperature control can influence both predicted and unforeseen impacts that then influence the results of mechanical properties. This comprehensive study explores the impact of CRs in diffusion, microstructural development, and the characterization of aluminum alloys and the influence of various manufacturing processes and post-process treatments, and it studies analytical models that can predict their effects. It examines a broad range of CRs encountered in diverse manufacturing methods, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), directed energy deposition (DED), casting, forging, welding, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP). For example, varying CRs might result in different types of solidification and microstructural evolution in aluminum alloys, which thereby influence their mechanical properties during end use. The study further examines the effects of post-process heat treatments, including quenching, annealing, and precipitation hardening, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. It discusses numerical and analytical models, which are used to predict and optimize CRs for achieving targeted material characteristics of specific aluminum alloys. Although understanding CR and its effects is crucial, there is a lack of literature on how CR affects alloy properties. This comprehensive review aims to bridge the knowledge gap through a thorough literature review of the impact of CR on microstructure and mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Advanced aluminides strengthened with incoherent Laves phase precipitates are promising lightweight and creep-resistant alternatives for high-alloy steels and superalloys for high-temperature critical components up to 750 °C service temperature. A significant issue with manufacturing these aluminides with conventional casting is the strong coarsening tendency of the Laves phase precipitates at elevated temperatures, leading to a significant strength reduction. In this context, the short lifetime of the melt pool in additive manufacturing and its fast solidification and cooling rates promise to consolidate these aluminides with homogeneously distributed fine Laves phase particles without coarsening. The main scientific objective of this work is to exploit the unique characteristics of the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process to print dense and crack-free bulk Fe3Al-1.5Ta samples containing uniformly distributed (Fe, Al)2Ta Laves phase precipitates. The Fe-25Al-2Ta (at.%) alloy was selected for this work since its creep resistance at 650 °C surpasses the one of the P92 martensitic–ferritic steel (one of the most creep-resistant alloys developed for steam turbine applications). Fundamentals on process–microstructure relationships governing the L-PBF-fabricated builds are provided by a detailed microstructural characterization using X-ray diffractometer (XRD) and ultra-high-resolution scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) and high-resolution electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detectors. Orientation imaging microscopy (OIM) and grain reference orientation deviation (GROD) maps were applied to measure texture and visualize substructures within the grains. The mechanism of voids formation, morphology, and volume fraction as a function of the input energy density was identified. The melting and solidification dynamics led to microstructures with large columnar grains, porosity, and periodic cracks during the printing process. Processing samples at the building temperatures below the brittle-to-ductile transition temperature, BDTT (750 °C), often caused severe macrocracking and delamination. Crack-free samples with densities higher than 99%, some approaching 99.5%, were fabricated from pre-alloyed gas-atomized powders with a combination of high laser power (250–300 W), slow-to-medium scanning speed (500–1000 mm/s), and 800 °C build plate preheating using a 67° rotation scanning strategy. The morphology of the pores in the volume of the samples indicated a relatively sharp transition from spherical geometry for scanning speeds up to 1000 mm/s to crack-like pores for higher values. The ultra-fast cooling during the L-PBF process suppressed D03 Fe3Al-ordering. The Fe3Al-1.5Ta builds were characterized by B2 FeAl-type order clusters dispersed within a disordered A2 α-(Fe, Al) matrix. Additionally, the (Fe, Al)2Ta Laves phase (C14–P63/mmc) was predominantly formed at the matrix phase grain boundaries and frequently dispersed within the grains. The quantitative EDX analysis of the matrix gave 77.6–77.9 at.% Fe, 21.4–21.7 at.% Al, and 0.6–0.8 at.% Ta, while the composition of the Laves phase was 66.3–67.8 at.% Fe, 8.7–9.8 at.% Al, and 22.4–24.9 at.% Ta, indicating that the Laves phase is considerably enriched in Ta with respect to the matrix. The L-PBF-fabricated alloys were characterized by coarse, columnar grains which grow epitaxially from the substrate, were several m in width, and extended across several layers along the building direction. The grains exhibited a relatively strong microtexture close to <0 0 1> with respect to the building direction. The L-PBF builds showed a bulk hardness value comparable to the as-cast and spark plasma-sintered counterparts. A negligible variation of the hardness across the build height was observed. Within the framework of this study, we demonstrated that the porosity and cracking issues could be resolved mainly by controlling the process parameters and preheating the build platform above the BDTT. Nevertheless, alloy modifications and/or post-manufacturing processing are required for microstructure refinement.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Multi-material laser powder bed fusion (MM-LPBF) offers the ability to locally tailor functional properties by combining dissimilar metals within a single component. However, achieving robust bonding at highly mismatched interfaces remains a critical challenge. This work investigates the interfacial evolution in CuCrZr&ndash;316LSS transitions, a material pair with extreme differences in thermal conductivity and a 75% difference in optimal volumetric energy density. This study investigates the interfacial formation mechanisms in CuCrZr&ndash;316LSS using five distinct interface configurations: (i) 316L deposited over CuCrZr across a horizontal interface, (ii) CuCrZr deposited over 316L across a horizontal interface, (iii) 316L deposited over CuCrZr along a diagonal interface, (iv) CuCrZr deposited over 316L along a diagonal interface, and (v) the two materials printed with a vertical interface via intralayer deposition. The results demonstrate that deposition order, i.e., laser scanning sequence, and interface geometry critically dictate the quality of interfaces in MM-LPBF systems. Microstructural characterization via optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, electron backscatter diffraction, and transmission electron microscopy revealed that exposure sequence strongly governs interfacial morphology, phase development, and the presence of interfacial defects. To further contextualize these results, meso-scale computational fluid dynamics simulations were employed to capture melt-pool dynamics, convection patterns, and material mixing behavior. Overall, this work clarifies the fundamental role of build orientation and laser scanning sequence in governing process stability and interface quality in MM-LPBF systems (copper- and iron-based in this study) and lays the foundation to achieve reliable interface quality in multi-material components manufactured through MM-LPBF.</jats:p>

The excerpt defines the secondary-electron yield as the number of emitted secondary electrons per primary electron and divides the signal into SEI and SEII contributions. SEI are generated by incident primary electrons as they pass through the escape zone, while SEII are generated by backscattered electrons leaving the sample. The stated yield relation is δ = δPE + ηδBSE = δPE(1 + βη), where δPE is the number of SE released per primary electron, δBSE is the number released per BSE, η is the BSE coefficient or fraction/number of BSE relative to primary electrons, and β = δBSE/δPE is the relative efficiency of BSEs for producing secondary electrons. Since BSEs approach the surface at favorable angles and have lower energies, β is greater than one and is typically 3–6. For a typical metal or semiconductor with η approximately 3.0, the excerpt states that less than 50% of the total SE signal is produced directly by incident electrons; thus the BSE-mediated SEII component supplies the remainder, subject to the precise meaning of η in the source notation. ## pqac-00000019

From text 'kawano2012applicationofthe pages 49-52'.

K Kawano. Application of the ultra high resolution, low voltage scanning electron microscopy in the materials science. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt explains charging through the balance between incident electrons accumulated in a specimen and electrons emitted from its surface. For insulating material, negative charging occurs when relatively few secondary and backscattered electrons are emitted compared with the number of electrons accumulated. The negatively charged region therefore appears bright in an In-lens secondary-electron image. This provides the relevant mechanism for why insulating particles such as alumina, silica, or SiC may show bright contrast: the particle’s insulating nature allows charge to build up, and the resulting surface potential changes the secondary-electron signal. However, the excerpt does not specifically discuss those three materials or establish that every bright particle is caused by charging. It also distinguishes detector behavior. In-lens images are strongly affected by charging, whereas SE2 images are less commonly affected because the SE2 signal combines secondary and backscattered electrons and the backscattered component is less sensitive to charging and edge effects. The excerpt therefore supports bright charging contrast most directly for In-lens/SE imaging. It does not establish that charging will make an insulating particle bright in both SE and BSE images; BSE-related contrast can be less affected, and composition, topography, crystallography, detector geometry, and charging conditions may all contribute.

It states that specimen charging affects secondary-electron (SE) images much more strongly than higher-energy backscattered-electron (BSE) images. Thus, charging can substantially alter the apparent brightness and contrast of an insulating particle in SE imaging. The discussion of low-loss electron imaging indicates that charging may produce reduced apparent charging in the detected signal, but this does not eliminate the physical charge: surface charging can still deflect the primary beam, and sufficiently strong charge buildup can cause beam deflection. BSE imaging is presented as a charge-mitigation approach because BSEs are less affected than SEs; BSE detection can therefore reduce charging-related image distortion, but the excerpt does not establish that an insulating particle will necessarily appear bright in both SE and BSE images. It also notes that conductive coatings can mitigate charging, while introducing artifacts and potentially changing surface details or dimensions, especially for nanoscale particles. Low landing energy, fast scanning, charge neutralization, and conductive sprays are listed as other mitigation methods.

The excerpt establishes that charging in nonconductive specimens can strongly modify SEM image formation. Negative charging can deflect the incident beam and change where electrons actually land, producing distorted or misleading contrast; in extreme cases, the beam may be diverted away from the specimen and generate signal from chamber components. For insulating particles such as alumina, silica, or SiC, a negative surface potential can plausibly make the particles appear bright in SE imaging because the electric field changes the trajectories of low-energy secondary electrons and can direct more of them toward the detector, whereas positive charging attracts secondary electrons back to the surface and makes the region dark. The excerpt explicitly states the darkening and SE loss associated with positive charging, but it does not directly quantify the SE enhancement caused by negative charging or explain BSE contrast. Charging can nevertheless affect BSE images indirectly by deflecting the primary beam, changing its landing position and energy, and altering the electrons reaching the detector. Thus, an insulating particle may appear bright in both SE and BSE images when charging simultaneously enhances detected signal and/or changes beam trajectories, but the provided passage does not explicitly document that specific SE-plus-BSE observation.

  Due to the way BSE signal is transmitted from
target to CRT  it is possible to preferentially treat
useful components of the total signal at the expense
of the rest. Several different types of 'signal pro-
cessing' are  available within the standard  con-
figuration of an SEM (Wells, 1974; Newbury, 1975):
black-level correction (D.C. suppression), intensity
modulation (gamma correction), image differentia-
tion and y-modulation. Of these, black-level cor-
rection  is perhaps most  useful  in BSE images
because it allows the background to the total signal
to be subtracted with a concomitant amplification
of the remainder. Similar effects may be achieved
via gamma correction.

  Atomic number and crystallographic contrast
 images with the SEM: a review of backscattered
                 electron techniques

                           GEOFFREY  E. LLOYD
                       Department of Earth Sciences, The University, Leeds LS2 9JT

                                              Abstract
Backscattered electrons (BSE) are incident electrons reflected back from a target specimen and imaged
with the scanning electron microscope (SEM). Three  distinct BSE signals  exist: atomic number or
Z-contrast, in which composition determines image contrast; orientation contrast, in which specimen
crystal structure determines image contrast; and electron channelling patterns (ECP), which are unique for
a particular crystal orientation. The origins of these three signals are described, with particular attention
being given to the necessary SEM operational and specimen preparation requirements. Z-contrast images
are relatively simple to obtain and also have a familiar appearance such that their usage should become
commonplace. ECP  in comparison require subsequent interpretation which depends on the crystal
structure and the relationship between crystal and specimen coordinate systems. A general solution to
ECP interpretation  is therefore presented, involving the construction of reference 'ECP-maps' over the
surface of a sphere. A brief summary of the applications and potential use of the three BSE signals in the
geological sciences  is also given.
KEYWORDS: contrast images, scanning electron microscopy, backscattered electrons.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'georgin2020advancedcharacterizationof pages 41-45'.

BMF Georgin. Advanced characterization of defect and grain structures in net-shape hot isostatically pressed in-718. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt defines the backscatter coefficient as η = iBSE/iPE, the ratio of detected backscattered-electron current to incident primary-electron current. It does not provide numerical η values for Al2O3, SiO2, SiC, or diamond at 5 kV, so those values would need to be obtained from experimental data, Monte Carlo simulations, or a BSE-yield reference. Qualitatively, above approximately 5 kV, BSE yield increases with atomic number and is relatively independent of incident energy; near and below 5 kV, η decreases and its dependence on atomic number becomes weaker. Below 1 kV, atomic-number contrast is described as nearly absent, while crystallographic channeling and topographic effects become more important. For a simple BSE contrast estimate, the stoichiometric mean atomic numbers can be calculated as: Al2O3 = (2×13 + 3×8)/5 = 10; SiO2 = (14 + 2×8)/3 = 10; SiC = (14 + 6)/2 = 10; and diamond C = 6. These arithmetic mean Z values are useful for rough comparison only, because actual BSE coefficients also depend on voltage, density, composition, detector geometry, and electron-scattering physics.


---

## pqac-00000034

From text 'lloyd1987atomicnumberand pages 3-5'.

Geoffrey E. Lloyd. Atomic number and crystallographic contrast images with the sem: a review of backscattered electron techniques. Mineralogical Magazine, 51:3-19, Mar 1987. URL: https://doi.org/10.1180/minmag.1987.051.359.02, doi:10.1180/minmag.1987.051.359.02. This article has 734 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides qualitative guidance for estimating BSE contrast but does not tabulate numerical backscatter coefficients for Al2O3, SiO2, SiC, or diamond at 5 kV. It defines q as the fraction of incident electrons that reappear as backscattered electrons and states that q generally increases with specimen atomic number. The article also reports little dependence of q on accelerating voltage, although q decreases slightly as voltage increases; therefore, low-voltage values may differ somewhat from values measured at higher beam energies. For a simple mean-atomic-number estimate using the stoichiometric, atom-weighted average Z, the compounds would be: Al2O3 = (2×13 + 3×8)/5 = 10; SiO2 = (1×14 + 2×8)/3 = 10; SiC = (14 + 6)/2 = 10; and diamond C = 6. These mean-Z values suggest similar first-order Z contrast for the three compounds, while diamond should have substantially lower BSE yield. However, actual compound BSE coefficients depend on beam energy, detector geometry, specimen density and composition, and should be obtained from experimental tables or a quantitative BSE model rather than inferred from mean Z alone. Surface roughness can also introduce topographic contrast and degrade compositional Z contrast.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'cousens2006amontecarlo pages 3-4'.

D. R. Cousens and D. C. Joy. A monte carlo study of the position of phase boundaries in backscattered electron images. Scanning, 19:547-552, Dec 2006. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/sca.4950190804, doi:10.1002/sca.4950190804. This article has 9 citations.

The excerpt describes a Monte Carlo model for estimating the backscatter coefficient at an interface, using the backscatter coefficients on either side of the interface and the SEM voltage. It does not provide numerical backscatter coefficients for bulk Al2O3 (alumina), SiO2 (silica), SiC (silicon carbide), or diamond carbon at 5 kV. It also does not list or calculate mean atomic numbers for these compounds. The text indicates that low-voltage results require caution: data at 1 kV were excluded from the fitted model because the fit was poor, and the stopping-power and scattering models were considered invalid at low kV. Thus, the excerpt cannot substantiate specific 5 kV coefficient values or compound mean-atomic-number estimates. It does establish that atomic number strongly affects the interface profile, especially near a high-Z/low-Z boundary, and that the model uses the coefficients of the materials on each side rather than a single compound coefficient. The figures concern interfaces between elemental atomic numbers 22 and 39, and 40 and 74, not the requested compounds.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'lin2007astudyof pages 133-137'.

Y Lin. A study of the secondary electrons. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt does not provide measured backscatter coefficients for Al2O3, SiO2, SiC, or diamond, nor does it list their mean atomic numbers. Its BSE data concern elemental Si, Sc, Ti, Cr, Cu, Ag, Au, and W, with measurements primarily between 0.8 and 3 keV. It states that BSE yield depends on atomic number Z and beam energy Eb and gives two empirical fitting approaches: the Neubert–Rogaschewski expression and the Hunger–Küchler form η(Z,Eb) = Eb raised to m(Z), multiplied by C(Z). These formulas are intended for normal incidence and specify Eb in keV, so estimating values at 5 kV would require applying or extrapolating the supplied fits. For compound contrast estimation, the excerpt provides no rule for selecting or calculating an effective/mean atomic number for compounds; that quantity would need to be obtained separately from the elemental composition and the chosen averaging convention. The figures and table can support comparison with elemental trends, but they do not directly answer the requested compound values.

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000043

From text 'lin2007astudyof pages 133-137'.

Y Lin. A study of the secondary electrons. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt concerns the backscattering coefficient (BSE yield, η) and gives empirical formulas for calculating η from atomic number Z and beam energy Eb, with Eb expressed in keV. It does not directly tabulate aluminum or iron values at 5 or 20 keV; the reproduced table only begins with silicon and measurements from 1.0–3.0 keV. The Neubert–Rogaschewski fit is given as a cubic polynomial in Z multiplied by an energy-dependent logarithmic correction, while the Hunger–Küchler fit expresses η as Eb raised to a Z-dependent exponent times a polynomial function of ln Z. For comparison, Al (Z=13) and Si (Z=14) are neighboring elements, so their calculated BSE coefficients should be close; the cubic-Z portion of the first fit gives Si a slightly higher value than Al at the reference energy Eb=20 keV (approximately 0.173 versus 0.161, subject to the excerpt’s OCR formatting). Iron has Z=26 and therefore a substantially larger coefficient than either Al or Si. The text specifically states that Si’s BSE yield decreases with increasing beam energy, while elements with Z above 29 show the opposite trend.


---

## pqac-00000044

From text 'kawano2012applicationofthe pages 61-70'.

K Kawano. Application of the ultra high resolution, low voltage scanning electron microscopy in the materials science. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt provides the aluminum backscatter coefficient only for the conditions specified in Table 2.2: a 5.0 kV acceleration voltage, a 70° incident angle, and a Monte Carlo simulation using 200,000 electrons. Under those conditions, the coefficient for aluminum is 0.491140, or approximately 49.114%. The corresponding magnesium value is 0.474820. The excerpt does not provide a 5 kV backscatter coefficient for iron (Fe), nor does it provide silicon (Si) values that would allow a numerical comparison between aluminum and silicon. It also does not contain a table of eta values for pure elements at both 5 keV and 20 keV. Therefore, the aluminum value can be reported directly, but Fe, Al-versus-Si comparisons, and the requested 5/20 keV pure-element eta dataset require another source or additional pages. The excerpt notes that backscatter coefficients vary with electron energy, atomic number, and incident angle; specifically, for aluminum, coefficients increase as the incident angle increases. Thus, the aluminum value should not be generalized to other geometries or energies without accounting for those parameters.


---

## pqac-00000045

From text 'kawano2012applicationofthe pages 203-208'.

K Kawano. Application of the ultra high resolution, low voltage scanning electron microscopy in the materials science. Unknown journal, 2012.

The excerpt provides aluminum backscattering coefficients at 5 kV for two incident angles. In Table 6.2, calculated for an incident angle of 0°, the coefficient for Al is 0.170720 (17.072%). In Table 6.3, calculated for an incident angle of 70°, the Al coefficient is 0.491140 (49.114%). Thus, the appropriate aluminum value depends on the measurement geometry. The excerpt introduces Table 6.4, which contains Fe and Mn backscattering coefficients from 0.5 to 5.0 kV, but the supplied text ends before the numerical table entries, so the Fe value at 5 kV cannot be identified here. No silicon coefficients or comparison between Al and Si are included. Likewise, the excerpt does not provide a general list of eta values for pure elements at 5 keV and 20 keV; only Al and Mg values through 5 kV, and the heading for Fe and Mn, are present. The tabulated values are Monte Carlo calculations using 200,000 electron trajectories.


---

## pqac-00000046

From text 'sim2005newtechniquefor pages 2-4'.

K. S. SIM and J. D. WHITE. New technique for in‐situ measurement of backscattered and secondary electron yields for the calculation of signal‐to‐noise ratio in a sem. Journal of Microscopy, 217:235-240, Mar 2005. URL: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2818.2005.01448.x, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2818.2005.01448.x. This article has 21 citations.

The excerpt defines the backscattered-electron yield (backscatter coefficient) as η = I_BSE/I_PE and states that the study measured η for Au, Si, Al, Cu, K, and In at 10, 20, and 30 keV. However, the supplied pages do not contain the complete numerical tables, and they provide no measurements at 5 keV. Therefore, exact backscatter coefficients for aluminum and iron at 5 kV cannot be extracted from this excerpt; iron is not among the materials listed in the reported measurements. The excerpt also does not show the 20-keV numerical entries for Al or Si, so a numerical Al-versus-Si comparison at 20 keV cannot be made from the supplied text. It does indicate that the reported BSE yields generally agree with Reimer and Tolkamp’s published values to within 10%, but this is a general accuracy statement rather than the requested element-specific values. The apparent table fragment begins with silicon at 10 keV (η = 0.185), but it does not include the corresponding Al or Si values at 20 keV.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table showing the estimated backscatter coefficients (eta) and mean atomic numbers for the materials requested at approximately 5 kV and 20 kV. The materials are: Al (Z=13), Si (Z=14), C diamond (Z=6), Al2O3, SiO2, SiC, Mg2Si, Fe (Z=26), beta-Al5FeSi, alpha-Al15(Fe,Mn)3Si2. For compounds, calculate the mass-fraction-weighted mean atomic number Z_bar. For pure elements at 20 kV, use the standard fit eta = -0.0254 + 0.016Z - 1.86e-4*Z^2 + 8.3e-7*Z^3 (Goldstein Eq 2.2). Note that at 5 kV, eta values are similar or slightly higher than at 20 kV for light elements (the difference is small). For compounds, use the mass-fraction average. Include columns: Material, Z_bar (mean atomic number), eta at ~20 kV (estimated from Z_bar), eta at ~5 kV (literature/estimated), Expected BSE brightness ordering. Note that exact 5 kV compound values are not widely tabulated and most entries are estimates. The key point is that the Z-ordering is preserved at 5 kV. Note: For Al2O3, Z_bar \u2248 10.6 (mass-fraction average); SiO2, Z_bar \u2248 10.8; SiC, Z_bar \u2248 10.0; Mg2Si, Z_bar \u2248 12.9; diamond C Z_bar = 6; Fe Z_bar = 26; beta-Al5FeSi Z_bar \u2248 15.2; alpha-Al15(Fe,Mn)3Si2 Z_bar \u2248 14.2."}

{"answer": "## SEM Imaging of As-Built LPBF AlSi10Mg: ETD Signal Composition, Z-Contrast, Charging, and BSE Coefficients at 5 kV

### (1) BSE-Derived Fraction of the ETD SE-Mode Signal

The Everhart–Thornley detector (ETD), when operated in SE mode with a positively biased Faraday cage (+300 V) and high scintillator potential (+10 kV), collects four distinct signal components: **SE1** (secondary electrons generated by the primary beam within the specimen escape depth), **SE2** (secondary electrons generated by backscattered electrons exiting the specimen surface), **SE3** (secondary electrons generated when BSEs strike the pole piece and chamber walls), and **direct BSE** (high-energy backscattered electrons that reach the scintillator directly) (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

Of these, SE2, SE3, and direct BSE are all derived from the backscattering process. The total secondary electron yield at the specimen can be written as:

**δ_total = δ_PE (1 + β·η)**

where δ_PE is the SE yield from primary electrons alone, η is the backscatter coefficient, and β = δ_BSE/δ_PE is the relative efficiency of BSE for producing secondary electrons, typically in the range 3–6 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004). The fraction of specimen-emitted SEs that are SE2 is therefore f_SE2 = β·η/(1 + β·η).

**SE3** has been reported to constitute approximately **10–50% of the secondary-electron signal** reaching a conventional ETD, depending strongly on working distance, pole-piece geometry, and chamber configuration (pqac-00000017). Griffin (2011) demonstrated that the pole piece, with its high effective incidence angle, can produce a dominant SE3 signal at short working distances (pqac-00000005). Peters (1982a, 1982b) developed an absorption plate placed over the pole piece to suppress SE3, demonstrating experimentally that a large part of the ETD SE signal is BSE-mediated. Direct BSE reaching the scintillator constitute a relatively small fraction of the positively biased ETD signal because the scintillator subtends a limited solid angle; however, the remote BSE that generate SE3 from the full chamber hemisphere represent a much larger effective collection area (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012).

The following table summarizes the ETD signal components:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Effect of a light matrix (Al, Z = 13) and low beam energy (5 kV):**

For aluminum at ~20 kV, η ≈ 0.152 (pqac-00000011). At 5 kV normal incidence, Monte Carlo calculations give η ≈ 0.171 for Al (pqac-00000045). With β ≈ 3–6, the product β·η for Al is approximately 0.45–0.90, meaning SE2 constitutes roughly 31–47% of the specimen-emitted SE signal. For iron (Z = 26, η ≈ 0.28 at 20 kV), β·η ≈ 0.84–1.68, and the SE2 fraction rises to 46–63% (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000011). Thus, even for a light matrix like Al, the BSE-derived SE fraction is substantial, though smaller than for heavier elements.

The total SE yield itself is Z-dependent through the SE2 term: since η increases monotonically with Z (at energies above ~2 keV), δ_total = δ_PE(1 + β·η) increases with Z via the β·η product (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000004). At low beam energies below approximately 2 keV, the backscatter coefficient begins to show anomalous behavior: η decreases for heavy elements (e.g., Au falls from ~0.5 at 10 keV to ~0.2 near 400 eV) and may increase slightly for light elements, potentially causing contrast compression or even reversal in the sub-keV regime (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010). At 5 kV, however, the standard monotonic Z-dependence of η is well preserved, and the η values are similar to or slightly higher than their 20 kV counterparts for light elements (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007).

---

### (2) Does an ETD SE-Mode Image Show Z-Contrast on a Flat Polished Specimen?

**Yes.** Goldstein et al. (2018) explicitly demonstrate that the positively biased ETD shows atomic-number (compositional) contrast on a polished cross section of Al-Cu aligned eutectic. The higher-Z phase (CuAl₂, Z̄ ≈ 25) appears brighter than the Al-2%Cu solid solution (Z̄ ≈ 13.2) in both the dedicated semiconductor BSE detector and the ETD (positive bias) (pqac-00000011). The text states: "although the SE1 signal of the E–T detector does not show predictable variation with composition, the BSE components of the E–T signal reveal the atomic number contrast" (pqac-00000011).

The dedicated BSE detector **enhances** the compositional contrast relative to the ETD because it has a more predictable, monotonic response to η and suppresses topographic and edge effects. The semiconductor BSE detector shows increased response from higher-energy BSEs, which are produced in greater relative abundance from heavier elements, thus further amplifying Z-contrast beyond the simple η difference (pqac-00000011). In the pyrite (FeS₂)/galena (PbS) example, the large Z difference is visible in both detectors, but "the topographic contrast is so strong [in the ETD image] that it overwhelms the compositional contrast" for rough specimens (pqac-00000014).

**It is therefore incorrect to state that ETD SE images "cannot tell whether a feature is heavier than the matrix."** On a flat, polished multiphase specimen where topographic contrast is minimized, the ETD in positive-bias mode carries substantial Z-contrast information through its BSE-derived signal components (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012). The Z-contrast in the ETD is, however, diluted compared to a dedicated BSE detector and can be obscured by topographic and edge effects on rough surfaces.

---

### (3) Other Mechanisms That Make Sub-Micron Features Bright in ETD Images

Besides higher mean atomic number, several mechanisms can produce bright contrast from sub-micron features in ETD images of a polished AlSi10Mg surface:

**a) Edge and topographic effects.** The secondary electron coefficient depends strongly on surface inclination as δ(θ) ≈ sec(θ), increasing rapidly as the beam approaches grazing incidence (pqac-00000012). Sub-micron particles that protrude even slightly above a polished surface, or that have steep edges due to differential polishing, will produce enhanced SE emission at their periphery, appearing as bright halos. This is a well-known artifact in ETD imaging and is explicitly described by Goldstein et al. (2018) (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**b) Negative charging of insulating particles.** Insulating particles such as Al₂O₃, SiO₂, SiC, or diamond embedded in a conducting Al matrix can accumulate negative charge when the incident beam energy is above the E₂ crossover energy (the energy at which total emitted yield equals unity). For alumina, E₂ ≈ 2.9–4.2 keV; for quartz, E₂ ≈ 3.0 keV (pqac-00000022). At 5 kV, which is near or above E₂ for these oxides, the specimen tends toward negative charging. A negative surface potential retards incoming primaries (reducing their effective landing energy) but also creates a local electric field that can accelerate SE away from the particle toward the positively biased ETD, making the particle appear anomalously bright (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023). Charge accumulation can produce fields of order 10⁷ V/cm at the surface (pqac-00000024), and the resulting bright or dark contrast can fluctuate temporally.

**c) Contamination.** Carbon contamination buildup under the beam creates a low-Z layer that generally reduces both SE and BSE yield, typically darkening features. However, differential contamination rates between phases can produce contrast artifacts.

**How strongly does BSE detector confirmation establish higher Z?**

When a dedicated BSE detector (such as the Thermo Fisher Apreo in-lens T1 or a retractable annular/CBS detector) shows the **same bright features with the same grayscale ordering** as the ETD, this provides strong evidence for compositional (Z) contrast rather than topographic or charging artifacts. The reasoning is:

- **BSE images are largely insensitive to specimen charging** because BSE have energies of keV, far exceeding any surface potential of a few volts; the low-energy SE that are most affected by charging are excluded by a BSE detector (pqac-00000020).
- **Topographic contrast is suppressed** by large-solid-angle, annular BSE detectors operated in SUM mode, because directionality differences from tilted surfaces are integrated out (pqac-00000014).
- **Edge enhancement is primarily an SE phenomenon** (sec θ dependence of δ), not a BSE effect; BSE detectors do not show the pronounced bright edge halos characteristic of SE images.

Therefore, when both the ETD and a dedicated BSE detector show the same bright features, the most parsimonious explanation is **higher mean atomic number** of those features relative to the matrix. However, this conclusion is not absolute: residual BSE topographic contrast from differential polishing relief remains possible even with a SUM-mode detector, and at very low kV, charging can indirectly affect BSE images by deflecting the primary beam and changing its landing energy (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). Confirmation by EDS point analysis or mapping is the definitive test.

---

### (4) Backscatter Coefficients and Ordering at 5 kV

The following table compiles estimated backscatter coefficients and brightness ordering for the phases relevant to AlSi10Mg microstructure:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Key findings:**

At 20 kV and above, the backscatter coefficient η increases monotonically with atomic number and can be estimated from the polynomial fit η = −0.0254 + 0.016Z − 1.86×10⁻⁴Z² + 8.3×10⁻⁷Z³ for E₀ ≥ 10 keV (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011). For compounds, η can be approximated from the mass-fraction-weighted average of elemental coefficients, or equivalently from the mass-fraction-averaged mean atomic number Z̄ inserted into the polynomial (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000034).

**Is the ordering preserved at 5 kV?** Above approximately 2 keV, the backscatter coefficient is described as "approximately independent of accelerating voltage" and monotonic with Z (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). Below 2 keV, η begins to show anomalous behavior: it decreases for heavy elements and may increase for light elements, with the normal Z-ordering potentially reversing in the sub-keV regime (gold at 100 eV can have η lower than aluminum) (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010). At 5 kV, the standard Z-ordering is expected to be fully preserved, with at most modest contrast compression among neighboring light elements.

For the specific case of Al vs. Mg₂Si at low voltage, CASINO Monte Carlo simulations showed that the BSE contrast between Al (η ≈ 0.200 at 1 keV) and Mg₂Si (η ≈ 0.190 at 1 keV) is very small at 1 keV but improves at 5 keV, where a 10 nm Mg₂Si precipitate could be detected with a 5 nm probe (pqac-00000016). This confirms that operating at 5 kV provides better Z-contrast than 1 kV for these light phases.

**Expected brightness ordering at 5 kV from darkest to brightest:**
C (diamond) < Al₂O₃ ≈ SiO₂ < SiC < Mg₂Si ≲ Al < Si ≪ β-Al₅FeSi ≈ α-Al₁₅(Fe,Mn)₃Si₂ ≪ Fe

The Fe-rich intermetallics (β-Al₅FeSi, α-Al₁₅(Fe,Mn)₃Si₂) have Z̄ ≈ 16–17 and should appear distinctly brighter than the Al matrix (Z = 13) in BSE images. Diamond and the oxide/carbide compounds (Z̄ ≈ 6–12) should appear darker than the Al matrix.

**Where evidence is missing:** Systematically measured, experimental BSE coefficients at exactly 5 kV for the specific compounds Al₂O₃, SiO₂, SiC, and the Al-Fe-Si intermetallic stoichiometries were not found in the literature accessed. The values in the table are estimates based on the mean-Z approximation and the well-established trends from Monte Carlo simulations. The Hunger–Küchler and Neubert–Rogaschewski empirical fits provide energy-dependent expressions for elemental η but have not been systematically validated for compounds at 5 kV (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000043). Lloyd (1987) noted that for minerals, observed Z-contrasts are typically less than 20% of the theoretically possible range, requiring signal processing (black-level correction) to visualize small compositional differences (pqac-00000028). This applies particularly to the closely spaced light phases in AlSi10Mg."}
